questions.explanation: Saggars shield ware from direct flame and ash.

questions.explanation: On-glaze enamels and lustres are fired on at lower temperatures.

options: too much plasticity in the clay

questions.stem: Unfired clay ware that is completely dry is called
questions.explanation: Greenware is unfired dry clay.

questions.explanation: Downdraught kilns give more even temperature.

questions.stem:
(a) State four properties of clay. [4 marks]
(b) A test bar of plastic clay is 15 cm long. After drying it is 14.1 cm and after firing 13.2 cm. Calculate (i) the drying shrinkage (ii) the total shrinkage, each as a percentage of the plastic length. [6 marks]
(c) Explain why grog may be added to a clay body. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Plasticity
1 mark: Shrinkage on drying and firing
1 mark: Porosity
1 mark: Refractoriness or hardness after firing
3 marks: Drying shrinkage = (15 - 14.1) / 15 x 100 = 6%
3 marks: Total shrinkage = (15 - 13.2) / 15 x 100 = 12%
2 marks: Grog (fired, ground clay) reduces shrinkage and warping
2 marks: Opens the body so it dries and fires evenly, reducing cracking
1 mark: Adds texture and strength, useful for large or sculptural work
questions.explanation: Clay is plastic, shrinks, is porous and becomes hard and refractory when fired. Drying shrinkage is 6% and total shrinkage 12%. Grog reduces shrinkage and cracking and adds texture.

questions.stem:
(a) Name four methods of applying glaze. [4 marks]
(b) State the colour obtained from each of the following oxides in an oxidising firing: (i) cobalt (ii) iron (iii) chromium (iv) manganese. [4 marks]
(c) Describe three glaze faults and their causes. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Dipping
1 mark: Pouring
1 mark: Spraying
1 mark: Brushing
1 mark: Cobalt: blue
1 mark: Iron: brown, amber or honey
1 mark: Chromium: green
1 mark: Manganese: purple-brown
3 marks: Crazing: network of cracks because the glaze shrinks more than the body
2 marks: Crawling: glaze rolls back leaving bare patches, due to dust, grease or thick application
2 marks: Pinholing or blistering: gas escape or over-firing
questions.explanation: Glaze is applied by dipping, pouring, spraying or brushing. Cobalt gives blue, iron brown, chromium green and manganese purple-brown. Faults include crazing, crawling and pinholing.

questions.topic: Hand building, wheel work and casting
questions.stem: Describe the production of a cylindrical vase by the slab method. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Wedge the clay to remove air and make it uniform
2 marks: Roll out an even slab using guide sticks and a rolling pin
2 marks: Cut a base and a rectangle for the wall using a template
2 marks: Allow slabs to stiffen to soft leather-hard
3 marks: Score and slip the edges, wrap the wall round and join it to the base, reinforcing with a coil
2 marks: Smooth the joints and refine the form; add decoration
2 marks: Dry slowly, bisque fire, glaze and glost fire
questions.explanation: Wedge, roll an even slab, cut parts from templates, stiffen, score and slip, join wall and base, smooth and decorate, then dry, bisque, glaze and fire.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the stages a kiln passes through during a bisque firing. [9 marks]
(b) State three ways of monitoring the temperature in a kiln. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Water-smoking stage: slow heating to drive out remaining physical water without bursting ware
3 marks: Decomposition stage: chemically combined water and organic matter burn off; careful heating through quartz inversion
3 marks: Maturing and cooling: ware hardens at final temperature, then kiln cools slowly before unpacking
2 marks: Pyrometric cones that bend at known temperatures
2 marks: Pyrometer with thermocouple
2 marks: Observing colour of the kiln interior through a spyhole, or draw trials
questions.explanation: Bisque firing passes through water-smoking, decomposition and maturing, then slow cooling. Temperature is monitored with cones, pyrometers and visual checks.

questions.stem:
(a) State five factors to consider in establishing a small-scale ceramic industry. [10 marks]
(b) Suggest five ways of marketing ceramic products. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Availability of raw materials such as clay
2 marks: Source of power and fuel
2 marks: Water supply
2 marks: Market and transport
2 marks: Capital, labour and government policy
1 mark: Exhibitions and trade fairs
1 mark: Social media and online stores
1 mark: Showrooms and retail outlets
1 mark: Advertisement in print, radio and television
1 mark: Supplying hotels, restaurants and gift shops
questions.explanation: A ceramic business needs raw materials, power, water, markets, transport, capital and labour. Products can be marketed through fairs, online, showrooms, adverts and hotel or gift-shop supply.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a museum and a gallery. [4 marks]
(b) Name two museums in Nigeria. [2 marks]
(c) Explain three ways in which museums are useful to a ceramics student. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Museum: collects, preserves, researches and displays objects of historical, cultural or scientific value
2 marks: Gallery: mainly displays and often sells works of art, usually contemporary
1 mark: National Museum, Lagos
1 mark: Another, e.g. Esie Museum, National Museum Benin, Jos Museum
3 marks: Study of ancient pottery forms and techniques for inspiration
3 marks: Research and documentation of materials and history
3 marks: Learning about preservation, display and appreciation of ceramic art
questions.explanation: A museum preserves and displays heritage; a gallery shows and sells art. Museums such as those in Lagos, Esie and Jos give students examples, research material and lessons in preservation.
